metadata.title: Shannon Shakes Hands with Chernoff: Big Data Viewpoint On Channel Information Measures

nodes.name: Channel capacity
nodes.statement: As a matter of fact, the channel capacity is defined as maximization mutual information.

nodes.name: Big data rules
nodes.statement: Two data rules are believed. For one thing, the data does not lie. For other thing, we only need to guarantee that our conclusion is correct with very large probability rather than one in the era of big data [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].
nodes.statement_short: Working premises: the data does not lie, and conclusions need only hold with very large probability.

nodes.name: Mutual information
nodes.statement: The mutual information is a measure of the amount of information that one random variable contains about another variable. In fact, it describes the reduction in the uncertainty of one random variable if another one is known [\cite{Elements}].
nodes.genus: a measure of the amount of information
differentia: that one random variable contains about another variable

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information
nodes.statement: According to [\cite{Elements}], the Shannon mutual information is defined as: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $X,Y$ are two random variables with marginal probability mass functions $p(x)$ and $p(y)$ and joint probability mass function $p(x,y)$.
nodes.statement_short: $I_S(X,Y)$ is the relative entropy between the joint distribution $p(x,y)$ and the product $p(x)p(y)$.

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information $I_S(X,Y)$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X,Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{x,y} {p(x,y)log{{p(x,y)} \over {p(x)p(y)}}} \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Shannon Information

nodes.name: Relative entropy (Kullback-Leibler distance)
nodes.statement: The relative entropy is given by [\cite{Elements}]: \begin{equation} D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}} \end{equation}

nodes.name: Relative entropy $D(p||q)$
nodes.statement: D(p||q) = \sum\limits_{x \in \textit{X}} {p(x)log{{p(x)} \over {q(x)}}}
nodes.label: KL distance

nodes.name: Chernoff Information
nodes.statement: Chernoff Information is the resulting error exponent when minimizing the overall probability of error [\cite{Elements}]. As defined in [\cite{Elements}], it is given by \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\alpha$ is real parameter with $0\leq \alpha \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff information is the error exponent of hypothesis testing, $-\min_{0\le\alpha\le1}\log\sum_x P_1^\alpha P_2^{1-\alpha}$.
differentia: when minimizing the overall probability of error

nodes.name: Chernoff information $I_C(P_1,P_2)$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C({{\rm{P}}_1},{P_2}) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Chernoff Information1

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: With the aid of Chernoff information to describe the relationship between the two variables, a new mutual information is defined as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} In this paper, we call it Chernoff mutual information relative to Shannon mutual information.
nodes.statement_short: Chernoff mutual information: the Chernoff information between $p(x,y)$ and $p(x)p(y)$.

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information $I_C(X,Y)$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} I_C(X,Y) \buildrel \Delta \over = - \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {\sum\limits_y {{p^\alpha }(x,y){{(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }}} } } \right). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Chernoff Information2

nodes.name: Shannon vs Chernoff mutual information differ in the divergence used
nodes.statement: In fact, both Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are to depict the inner relationship between two random variables. The difference is that they adopt different measures of the distance between two distributions. The relative entropy is adopted in Shannon mutual information and the R{\'{e}}nyi divergence is used in Chernoff mutual information [\cite{van2014renyi}].

nodes.name: Binary symmetric channel (BSC)
nodes.statement: Consider the BSC, which is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelBSC}. It is a binary channel where the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$. The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $.
differentia: the probability of the input symbols is $(\lambda,1-\lambda)$
The transmission error in it is $\varepsilon $

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = H(Y) - H(Y|X) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^2 {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^2 {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr & = (1 - \varepsilon )\log {{1 - \varepsilon } \over {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon }} + \varepsilon \log {\varepsilon \over {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )}}. \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Closed form of $I_S(X;Y)$ for the BSC in terms of $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$.
nodes.label: BSC Mutual information

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the BSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {P_1^\alpha (x)P_2^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ &=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log ( {(1 - \varepsilon )^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda (1 - \varepsilon ) + (1 - \lambda )\varepsilon } \right)^{1 - \alpha }} \\ &+ {\varepsilon ^\alpha }{\left( {\lambda \varepsilon + (1 - \lambda )(1 - \varepsilon )} \right)^{1 - \alpha }} ) \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: $I_C(X;Y)$ for the BSC as a minimization over $\alpha$ with no closed form.
nodes.label: BSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: No explicit solution for the BSC Chernoff mutual information
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, there is no explicit solution for Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}). As a result, it is arduous to analyze the Chernoff mutual information.\\ It is observed that the Shannon mutual information seems to be completely different from the Chernoff mutual information.

nodes.name: Multiple symmetric channel (MSC)
nodes.statement: The MSC is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:channelMBSC}. The number of input symbol is $M$. The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$).The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$.
differentia: The number of input symbol is $M$
The probability of the input symbol is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,...,\lambda_M)$ with $\lambda_1+\lambda_2+...+\lambda_M=1$ ($\lambda_i>0$)
The transmission error of each one is $\frac{\varepsilon}{M-1}$

nodes.name: Shannon mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & I_S(X;Y) = D(p(x,y)||p(x)p(y)) \cr & = \sum\limits_{k = 1}^M {\sum\limits_{j = 1}^M {p({x_k},{y_j})log{{p({x_k},{y_j})} \over {p({x_k})p({y_j})}}} } \cr \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Mutual information

nodes.name: Chernoff mutual information of the MSC
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &I_C(X;Y)=- \mathop {\min }\limits_{0 \le \alpha \le 1} \log \left( {\sum\limits_x {{p(xy)}^\alpha (x){(p(x)p(y))}^{1 - \alpha }(x)} } \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: MSC Chernoff information

nodes.name: ACE residual error $e^2$
nodes.statement: Assume random variables $X_1,X_2,\cdots ,X_p$ are predictors and $Y$ is response. Supposing $\phi _1(X_1),\phi _2(X_2),\cdots,\phi _p(X_p),\theta (Y)$ are arbitrary zero mean functions of the corresponding variables, the residual error is \begin{equation} {e^2}\left( {\theta ,{\phi _1},\cdots,{\phi _p}} \right) = {{E\left\{ {{{\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right]}^2}} \right\}} \over {E\left[ {{\theta ^2}(Y)} \right]}} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Normalized mean-square residual $e^2$ of $\theta(Y)$ against $\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)$ for zero-mean transformations.

nodes.name: ACE Algorithm
nodes.statement: \caption{ACE Algorithm} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\ \STATE For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\ \STATE End Inner Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\ \STATE End Outer Iteration Loop;\\ \STATE $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Alternating conditional expectations: iterate the $\phi_k$ updates until $e^2$ stops decreasing, then update $\theta$, until convergence.
nodes.label: alg:ACE

nodes.name: Functional relation between channel parameters and channel information
nodes.statement: Let $X_1,X_2,\cdots,X_p$ be the channel parameters and $Y$ be measured value of channel information. The functional relation between them is: \begin{equation} Y = f({X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Channel parameters known and independent; $f$ known
nodes.statement: It is supposed that ${X_1},{X_2},...,{X_p}$ are known and independent. Moreover, the functional relation $f$ is also known since it is defined by human to describe the channel information.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition of channel information
nodes.statement: Therefore, it is easy to get $Y$ and they form a data set $\{Y,X_1,\cdots,X_p\}$. This data set meets the precondition of the ACE algorithm, so ACE algorithm can be used to analyze them. As a result, one can get \begin{equation} \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta \end{equation} where $\delta$ is residual error.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\{Y,X_1,\dots,X_p\}$ satisfies ACE's precondition, ACE yields $\theta(Y)=\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)+\delta$, separating each parameter's influence.
assumptions: This data set meets the precondition of the ACE algorithm

nodes.name: ACE decomposition $\theta(Y) = \sum_i \phi_i(X_i) + \delta$
nodes.statement: \theta (Y) = \sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}(X_i)} + \delta
nodes.label: ACE_Def

nodes.name: Simulation Procedure
nodes.statement: \caption*{Simulation Procedure} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \STATE Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$; \STATE Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information; \STATE Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm; \STATE Repeat above process till the required times. \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Monte Carlo: sample channel parameters, compute the information measures, decompose them by ACE, repeat.
nodes.label: alg:simulated

nodes.name: BSC simulation
nodes.statement: $20000$ observations geneated from the Eq.(\ref{BSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{BSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$ are independently drawn from a uniform distribution $U(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with two input parameters.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition results on BSC are excellent
nodes.statement: The ACE algorithm is applied to this simulated data set and the results is shown in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda)+\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is extremely close to $1$. Furthermore, The error of the ACE decomposition $\delta$ is invariably near to zero. Clearly, both of them have shown that the ACE decomposition results are excellent.

nodes.name: BSC: ACE transformations coincide for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: It is noted that function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition. As a result, in the range of the errors permitted, the $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ appears to be coincided with each other. $\phi_1(\lambda)$ is monotone decreasing function. The greater $\lambda$, the faster the decline in $\phi_1(\lambda)$. Furthermore, $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ is symmetric around the line $\varepsilon = 0.5$ for the fact that the channel is symmetrical about $\varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: For the BSC, $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ are the same for both measures; $\phi_1$ decreases, $\phi_2$ is symmetric about $\varepsilon=0.5$.
assumptions: $\lambda$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error
conclusions: function curve of $\phi_1(\lambda)$ and $\phi_2(\varepsilon)$ w.r.t. Shannon mutual information is almost coincided with that w.r.t Chernoff mutual information after the ACE decomposition

nodes.name: BSC: Shannon values smaller than Chernoff, same trend
nodes.statement: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole variant trend is identical. $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.
conclusions: The results of Shannon mutual information are smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole variant trend is identical

nodes.name: MSC simulation
nodes.statement: $60000$ observations generated from the Eq.(\ref{MSC Mutual information}) and Eq.(\ref{MSC Chernoff information}) where $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ is the probability of the input symbol and $\varepsilon$ is the transmission error. They are generated randomly and independently, which is bound in $(0,1)$. In this case, our channel information is a multivariate case with four input parameters.

nodes.name: ACE validity confirmed again on MSC
nodes.statement: Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I} shows similar characteristics that in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I}. The value of the ACE decomposition error $\delta$ is still very small. On the other hand, the correlation between $\theta(y)$ and $\phi_1(\lambda_1)+\phi_2(\lambda_2)+\phi_3(\lambda_3)+\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is close to $1$. These two points verify the validity of the ACE algorithm again.

nodes.name: MSC: ACE transformations coincide for Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: It is obviously that the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures. It is worth noting that the minimum of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ occurs when $\varepsilon \approx 0.75$. The values of $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is big when $\varepsilon$ is very close to $0$ or $1$. Moreover, $\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$ and $\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ are very similar. Their function curve is flat and close to zero when the independent variable (the probability of the input symbol) is less than $0.7$ . When the independent variable approaches to $1$, the values of them rapid decrease. In fact, it is reasonable because these input variables are equivalent for the channel.
nodes.statement_short: For the MSC all five ACE transformations agree across the two measures; $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ is minimal near $0.75$ and the $\phi_i(\lambda_i)$ are alike.
conclusions: the function curves of $\theta(y)$,$\phi_1(\lambda_1)$,$\phi_2(\lambda_2)$,$\phi_3(\lambda_3)$ and $\phi_4(\varepsilon)$ are almost the same for these two channel information measures

nodes.name: MSC: Shannon values smaller than Chernoff, same trend
nodes.statement: As illustrated in Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, the result of Shannon mutual information is smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole varying trend is identical. $\theta(y)$ increases rapidly when $y$ is also close to zero and the slope of its curve is becoming smaller as $y$ increases.
conclusions: the result of Shannon mutual information is smaller than the Chernoff mutual information, but whole varying trend is identical

nodes.name: Big data viewpoint and the PAC model justify numerical analysis by ACE
nodes.statement: In this section, we analyze these ACE simulated results from the viewpoint of big data. There are several nature behind it. First of all, the data does not lie. Naturally, the ACE results can provide much true and useful information for us. Furthermore, we always turn to numerical analysis when it is difficult to do theoretical analysis. The complicated equations of Shannon or Chernoff mutual information are arduous to do intuitive theory analysis, especially when they are multivariable, so it is quite appropriate to do numerical analysis by ACE algorithm. In fact, the probably approximately correct (PAC) model is enough for us in most of time [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}]. In this model, one only need to construct algorithms which guarantee that it is correct with high probability (not necessarily one). This model is the foundation of Support Vector Machine (SVM) [\cite{vapnik2006estimation}].
nodes.statement_short: Numerical ACE analysis is justified because the data does not lie and PAC-style high-probability correctness suffices.

nodes.name: ACE results: only $\theta$ differs between Shannon and Chernoff
nodes.statement: The ACE results is \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $Y$ is the channel information and ${\textbf{X}}$ is all the set of all the input channel parameters. The equation ($a$) holds because the residual error $\delta$ can be ignored. From the figures above, it is noted that $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information. For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$. The function $\psi(\cdot)$ is different and ${\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} $ is the same.
nodes.statement_short: ACE gives $Y=\theta^{-1}(\sum_i\phi_i(X_i))=\psi(\varphi(\mathbf X))$ with $\varphi$ shared by Shannon and Chernoff and only $\psi$ differing.
assumptions: the residual error $\delta$ can be ignored
conclusions: $ \phi_i(X_i)$ is almost the same for both Shannon and Chernoff mutual information
For these two measures, the only difference is $\theta(\cdot)$

nodes.name: ACE result $Y = \psi(\varphi(\mathbf{X}))$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} Y = f\left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \overset{(a)}{=}{\theta ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})} } \right)= \psi \left( {\varphi \left( { {\textbf{X}} } \right)} \right)\\ \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Res_Fun

nodes.name: Shannon's $\theta^{-1}$ is bigger than Chernoff's
nodes.statement: From the Fig.\ref{fig:BSC C and I} to Fig.\ref{fig:MSC C and I}, it is also noted that the function $\theta(\cdot)$ is monotonic function. As mentioned above, the curves of $\theta(\cdot)$ have the same trend and the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information. Therefore, the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's. Actually, the facts extremely agree with the this corollary, which can well explain the phenomena in Fig.\ref{fig:BSC1 C and I}.
nodes.statement_short: Because $\theta$ is monotone and Shannon's $\theta(Y)$ is always below Chernoff's, Shannon's $\theta^{-1}$ is the larger.
assumptions: the values of $\theta(Y)$ for Shannon mutual information is invariably smaller than those for Chernoff information
conclusions: the Shannon's $\theta^{-1}(\cdot)$ is bigger than Chernoff's

nodes.name: Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff
nodes.statement: In this sense, Shannon shakes hands with Chernoff. Over the last decades, Shannon information and Chernoff information are always considered to be two kinds of channel information measures and the relation between them is that Kullback-Leibler divergence is the special case of R{\'{e}}nyi divergence when $\alpha=1$. The channel information measures deduced from them look very different even for the channel as simple as BSC. However, with the aid of the ACE algorithm, we find the inner relations between them. In fact, they are different metrics of the same physical quantity. For a channel, in a certain time, if all of its parameters are given, all of its state and properties will be determined. Thus the information about the same channel is always consistent. For example, the kilometer and centimeter are both measures of length, but they are used in different situations for convenience. Generally speaking, we do not adopt the centimeter to measure the distance between two cities. In contrast, we would like adopt it to measure the length of the steel rule. Their true values are identical when measuring the same things, even their numerical values are different. Similarly, the Shannon and Chernoff information are two metrics of the same quantity of information.
nodes.statement_short: Shannon and Chernoff mutual information are two metrics of the same channel information quantity, like kilometres and centimetres.
conclusions: they are different metrics of the same physical quantity
the Shannon and Chernoff information are two metrics of the same quantity of information

nodes.name: Nature of channel information $\varPsi$
nodes.statement: In this paper, we take $\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}}\right)$ as the nature of channel information and we get \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where the $\varPsi$ is the nature of channel information. It is only decided by the channel parameters and it contains the core of the channel information.
nodes.statement_short: $\varPsi=\varphi(\mathbf X)$, the measure-independent inner function of the channel parameters, is the nature of channel information.

nodes.name: Nature of channel information $\varPsi = \varphi(\mathbf{X})$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \varPsi=\varphi \left( {\textbf{X}} \right) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Nature_Fun

nodes.name: Every channel information measure is a function of $\varPsi$
nodes.statement: The other physical quantity about channel information is just the function of $\varPsi$, just as \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information.
assumptions: $\rm{I}$ is a measurement of channel information

nodes.name: Channel information measure $\mathrm{I} = \psi(\varPsi)$
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \rm{I}= \psi (\varPsi) \end{aligned}
nodes.label: Nature_Fun1

nodes.name: Shannon and Chernoff as compound functions with common inner $\varPsi$
nodes.statement: As far as Shannon mutual information and Chernoff mutual information are concerned, their only difference is the function $\psi(\cdot)$. They can be seen as a compound function. The inner is $\varPsi$ which is the function w.r.t. channel parameters and the outer is the function w.r.t. $\varPsi$. For different channel information measures, the inner is always the same but the outer is different.

nodes.name: ACE decomposition conjecture for new information measures
nodes.statement: There is a conjecture that if a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information, it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent.
nodes.statement_short: Any new channel information measure will decompose under ACE into a function of the same nature $\varPsi$.
assumptions: a novel information measure is put forward to measure the channel information
conclusions: it will be decomposed to a function of $\psi(\cdot)$ by ACE algorithm from a very large extent

nodes.name: Uses of the conjecture: judging and constructing information measures
nodes.statement: This rule can be used to judge the rationality of the new information measure. This conjecture also provides a way for us to propose a new information measure for the fact that we can construct that based on designing the function $\psi(\cdot)$. In fact, even if this guess is not right with probability one, the new one which conforms to the law is correct with large probability and we can easily find the relation between that and previous information measures, such as Shannon and Chernoff information.
nodes.statement_short: The conjecture gives a rationality criterion for new measures and a recipe for building them by designing $\psi$.

nodes.name: Initialize $\theta$ and $\phi_i$
nodes.statement: set $\theta (Y) = Y/\left\| Y \right\|$ and ${\phi _1}({X_1}),...,{\phi _p}({X_p}) = 0$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Start with $\theta(Y)=Y/\|Y\|$ and all $\phi_i=0$.

nodes.name: Outer iteration until $e^2$ stops decreasing
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\
nodes.statement_short: Outer loop: repeat until the residual error $e^2$ fails to decrease.

nodes.name: Inner iteration until $e^2$ stops decreasing
nodes.statement: Iterate until $e^2(\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p)$fails to decrease;\\
nodes.statement_short: Inner loop: repeat until $e^2$ fails to decrease.

nodes.name: For each $k$, update $\phi_k$ by conditional expectation
nodes.statement: For $k=1$ to p Do:\\ \begin{equation*} {\phi _{k,1}}({X_k}) = E\left[ {\theta (Y) - \sum\limits_{i \ne k} {{\phi _i}\left( {{X_i}} \right)} \left| {{X_k}} \right.} \right]; \end{equation*} replace $\phi_k(X_k)$ with $\phi_{k,1}(X_k)$;\\ End For Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: For $k=1..p$ set $\phi_k(X_k)=E[\theta(Y)-\sum_{i\ne k}\phi_i(X_i)\mid X_k]$.

nodes.name: End inner iteration loop
nodes.statement: End Inner Iteration Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: Close the inner loop.

nodes.name: Update $\theta$ by normalized conditional expectation
nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} {\theta _1}(Y) = {{E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1} {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \over {\left\| {E\left[ {\sum\limits_{i = 1}^p {{\phi _i}({X_i})\left| Y \right.} } \right]} \right\|}}; \end{equation*} replace $\theta(Y)$ with $\theta_1(Y)$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Set $\theta(Y)$ to the normalized $E[\sum_i\phi_i(X_i)\mid Y]$.

nodes.name: End outer iteration loop
nodes.statement: End Outer Iteration Loop;\\
nodes.statement_short: Close the outer loop.

nodes.name: Return the optimal transformations
nodes.statement: $\theta,\phi_1,...,\phi_p$ are the solution $\theta^*,\phi^*_1,...,\phi^*_p$;\\
nodes.statement_short: Output $\theta^*,\phi_1^*,\dots,\phi_p^*$.

nodes.name: Generate channel parameters
nodes.statement: Generate channel parameters, such as $\lambda$ and $\varepsilon$;
nodes.statement_short: Sample the channel parameters.

nodes.name: Calculate channel information measures
nodes.statement: Calculate the channel information measures, such as Shannon mutual information;
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the information measures on the sampled parameters.

nodes.name: Decompose by ACE
nodes.statement: Decompose these channel information measures by ACE algorithm;
nodes.statement_short: Run the ACE algorithm on the generated data set.

nodes.name: Repeat
nodes.statement: Repeat above process till the required times.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat the procedure the required number of times.
